records.name: Become a block captain
records.summary: Any resident can step up as captain of their own block: gather neighbors' signatures on a petition, then organize cleanups of the street alongside the Philadelphia More Beautiful Committee.
records.what_you_do: Captains sweep sidewalks and gutters, plant flowers and street trees, host block parties, and help neighbors keep up with trash and recycling days. They also organize block cleanups with the Philadelphia More Beautiful Committee (PMBC), which can supply tools and cleaning materials.

schedule.text: Saturday clean block events run March through August, scheduled by police district. Participating blocks hold three organized cleanups in the summer.

cost.text: The page lists no fee. PMBC provides cleanup supplies such as trash bags and street brooms.

first_step.how: Call PMBC at (215) 685-3971 to ask for a clean block petition, or use its online form. The petition is mailed to you. Collect signatures from 51 percent of the residents on your block, then mail the petition back to PMBC.
first_step.basis: The page says any resident can be a block captain and gives a clear way in: request a petition, collect signatures, and mail it back.
first_step.what_to_expect: The first stretch is paperwork. You get a petition in the mail, collect neighbors' signatures, and mail it back, and then a clean block officer contacts you to get started. Once the block is set up, the work is outdoors: summer cleanups with PMBC, plus reminders about trash and recycling days.
first_visit_tips: Count households first: only one adult signature per household counts toward the 51 percent.
Clean block officers keep Monday to Saturday hours, 7:30 am to 3:30 pm, from March through October, so call then.
Ask the same number whether your block already has a captain.

records.notes: The March 2026 Block Captain Rally post on the PMBC page sets the sign of life. The page gives no 2026 cleanup dates. The phone number is PMBC's main line; the page says clean block officers have their own numbers by police district.

records.name: Belmont Plateau Trails Alliance
records.summary: A group that works with the City and the Fairmount Park Conservancy to look after the trails on Belmont Plateau in West Fairmount Park.
records.what_you_do: Works on the trail system alongside the City and the Conservancy. The site does not say how members of the public can help.

first_step.how: Email Parks and Recreation's stewardship office (pprstewardship@phila.gov) and ask to be connected with this Friends group.
first_step.basis: The group's own site says its full site is coming soon, so the only way in is an email to the city office. The way in is unclear.

records.notes: belmonttrails.org says its full site is coming soon, and /about returned a 404, so no volunteer, event, cost or meeting details could be read. Status and sign of life are carried over from the city listing. A single web search found a Fairmount Park Conservancy Earth Day workday at the Plateau on April 22 (1 to 4 pm), which another listing ties to 2026. The Conservancy hosted it, not this group, so it is not used in this record. The Conservancy stays in leads_only for future research because it is a separate organization outside this batch.

records.name: Ben Franklin Mob H3
records.summary: A Philadelphia hash running group. A rotating hare lays a trail, and runners follow it at any pace, often in costume.
records.what_you_do: Follow a marked trail laid by a rotating hare at your own pace. Bring $10 in Hash Cash and photo ID.

schedule.text: Thursday trail runs: gather at 7 pm and run at 7:30 pm. The meeting place changes from trail to trail.

cost.text: Bring $10 in Hash Cash. The site does not say what it covers.

first_step.how: Read the About page (the New? link on the site) to learn how a first run works, then sign up for the weekly trail email from the Mail link.
first_step.basis: The site has a New? page that explains a first run and says all paces are welcome, and the trails are set to suit slower runners.
first_step.what_to_expect: Expect about 1 to 1.5 hours and 3 to 5 miles, at any pace, in any weather. The run ends at a bar, where the group gathers and sings afterward, and beer is central to the group.
first_visit_tips: Bring $10 in Hash Cash and photo ID.
Bring a headlamp; the site calls it a cranium lamp.
Dress for the weather, since runs go in any weather.
Check the weekly trail email, because the meeting place changes from trail to trail.

records.notes: The home page lists 2026 events (a 10/17/2026 relay and an 11/22/2026 event), which set the sign of life. The trail page gives 37 E Palmer St for the meeting place, but its map link shows 37 W Palmer St, so confirm before going. Neither page says whether walkers can join or what the Hash Cash covers. No minimum age is stated, and the runs end at a bar.

records.name: Bicycle Club of Philadelphia
records.summary: An all-volunteer nonprofit that promotes biking in the Philadelphia area and runs free group rides for every speed and skill level.
records.what_you_do: Pick a ride from the club's ride calendar at your speed and join it. Come to the monthly club meeting if you want to get more involved.

schedule.text: Rides run on a published ride calendar on most days of the week, at all speeds. Sunday rides leave at 12 noon from the Azalea Garden entrance behind the Art Museum. The club meets on the second Wednesday of the month at 6:30 pm, unless noted otherwise.

locations.label: Roxborough Memorial Hospital, ground floor conference room (monthly club meeting)

cost.text: Group rides are free. Club membership is $20 a year; student membership is $10 a year.

requirements.gear: Helmet (required), a bike in working order, a flat repair kit, a frame pump, a water bottle, and some ID.

first_step.how: Go to the Sunday noon Sunny Sunday D ride at the Azalea Garden formal entrance, behind the Art Museum. The club calls it a casual ride for people new to group riding. Non-members can ride, and you can join the club later through its Join BCP link.
first_step.basis: The club runs a beginner class on the second Sunday of the month (March to October) and a casual introductory Sunday ride, and it says non-members are welcome on rides.
first_step.what_to_expect: Rides are grouped by speed, and the club tells newcomers to start a level below what they expect. Listed times are departure times, so arrive 10 to 15 minutes early. A volunteer ride leader picks the route, and the helmet rule applies on club rides.
first_visit_tips: Wear a helmet. The club requires one.
Bring a flat repair kit, a frame pump, water, and ID.
Check the ride's meeting spot on the calendar, since spots vary by ride.

records.notes: The beginner class page and the October 2026 ride calendar give different meeting spots for the Sunday D ride (Italian Fountain on the class page, Azalea Garden formal entrance on the calendar). The record uses the calendar. Dues come from the register page. Newcomer rating raised from 3 to 5 under the rubric because of the beginner class.

records.name: Bicycle Coalition Youth Cycling (BCYC)
records.summary: A cycling team program for teens ages 12 to 18, run by the Bicycle Coalition of Greater Philadelphia. Riders start in a Core program at partner sites, then can move up to All Star teams in road, mountain bike, race, triathlon, or cyclocross.
records.what_you_do: Riders go to practices and events such as group rides, and can join a youth advisory council. Volunteers help at events, join practices, and keep athletes' bikes in good shape through the BCYC Pit Crew and Pedal Partner roles. The group pays its coaches and does not require racing experience for them.

schedule.text: Core teams meet at partner sites. All Star teams run in summer and fall. Practice days and times are not published.

cost.text: Athlete fees are not stated on the page. Riders are outfitted with equipment from community and sponsor donations.

first_step.how: Fill in the online youth application linked from the program page. Staff follow up about team placement.
first_step.basis: A public online application comes first, and the page does not describe a first practice. The Core level is the entry point for new riders, which helps, but the application comes before any contact.
first_step.what_to_expect: Riders begin in the Core program at one of eight partner sites, with practices and events such as group rides. Moving up to an All Star team, which runs in summer and fall, takes meeting attendance goals and passing written and on-bike tests, according to a 2024 post on the group's site. All Stars can take a bike home while they stay active in the program.
first_visit_tips: Ask staff which partner site is closest to you when they follow up about placement.
Email habib@bicyclecoalition.org or call 215-242-9253 with questions about the program.
If you would rather help first, use the volunteer interest form on the volunteer page.

records.notes: The program page lists the Philly Bike Ride (Oct 18, 8:30 am to 1 pm, year not shown) and a 2027 edition. These are one time events, so they are left out of the schedule. The All Star article is a June 2024 post, so its details may be old. The 2026 Hunting Park Hustle recap on the program page supports the 2026 sign of life. The September 2026 month is carried over from tier 1; the Roll Wit It ride date has no year on the page. Practice days, tryout dates, parent requirements and athlete fees are not stated. The volunteer page gives no minimum age for the Pedal Partner or Pit Crew roles. Newcomer rating lowered from 3 to 2 under the rubric because an application comes first.

records.name: Big Brothers Big Sisters Independence Region
records.summary: A mentoring agency for Philadelphia and six nearby counties in Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Adult volunteers, called Bigs, spend regular time with one child through a one-to-one mentoring program.
records.what_you_do: Bigs take part in one-to-one mentoring through one of several programs. Community-based mentoring means outings with a child who is picked up at home. Site-based mentoring happens at a site. Beyond School Walls is one-on-one time during the school day with mentors from partner companies. The LGBTQ+ programs include school groups and Rainbow Bigs. POWER Up is staff-led mentoring in partner schools. A visit lasts about two hours, at least twice a month. Bigs must be 21 or older.

schedule.text: Visits last about two hours, at least twice a month, for a term of at least one year. The site also mentions 18 months, so ask for the exact term.

cost.text: The site does not state a cost for becoming a Big.

first_step.how: Fill in the short interest form on the Be a Big page, then book the virtual interview with a staff member. The application and background checks come after that.
first_step.basis: The steps are listed clearly, but a person must do an interview, an application and background checks before they can see the program up close.
first_step.what_to_expect: Your first contact is a short interest form and a virtual interview with a staff member. After the application and background checks, you are matched with a Little, a child aged 7 and up, and begin regular outings of about two hours at least twice a month.
first_visit_tips: If you live outside Philadelphia city, you need a car.
The Philadelphia office is on the 5th floor at 100 North 20th Street.
Call (215) 790-9200 with questions before you fill in the form.

records.notes: The Be a Big page gives visits as about 2 hours on one line and 2 to 4 hours on another, and frequency as at least twice a month and 2 to 4 times a month. The term is one year on one line and at least 18 months on another. The record uses the lower wording and tells the visitor to ask. /faq returned a 404 and the site has no FAQ link. audience.min_age is left blank on purpose: the 21 age rule applies to Bigs, and a minimum age would hide public events from younger visitors. The events page lists a Quizzo night on October 28, 2026 and a Bowl for Kids Sake on November 15, 2026, both open to the public, and a Big Futures Breakfast listed for April 7, 2027. Event details are not recorded because they are one time events. Access and language support are not stated.

records.name: Black Spatial Relics
records.summary: An arts project that supports emerging and mid-career artists, especially Black artists, with residencies, grants, and gatherings. Much of its work is new performance about slavery, justice, and freedom.
records.what_you_do: Join the newsletter to hear about open calls and public events. Artists apply to the artist in residence program, the Conjure Council fund, or the micro grants when a call is open. The 2025 Conjure Council nominations closed in December 2025, so watch the newsletter for the next call.

first_step.how: Join the newsletter from the Join Newsletter link on the site. Then ask by email (blackspatialrelics@gmail.com) which public events are coming, since the Upcoming Events page lists only a 2023 event.
first_step.basis: The newsletter is open to anyone, but the site lists no current public event and does not say how to register for one, so the way in is unclear.
first_step.what_to_expect: The site does not describe a typical event, so check each listing for time, place and cost. Some past events were set aside for Black participants, and the Conjure Council fund is for artists and cultural workers who are descendants of the African Diaspora. The 2023 lab that appears on the events page was free.
first_visit_tips: Check whether an event is open to the public before you RSVP.
Email blackspatialrelics@gmail.com with questions about who can attend.

records.notes: Tier 1 tagged this group as history and heritage with preservation_architecture. The site describes performance work, so the tags were changed to theater-dance-performance with community_theater and storytelling_spoken_word. Kind is kept as nonprofit, but the site says it is a fiscally sponsored project of The Public Trust, so a reviewer may want to check it. The site names no street address or headquarters, so no location is recorded. The Upcoming Events page lists only a July 2023 lab, and the updates page stops at April 2023. Status rests on the March 2026 awardee announcement on the 2025 Conjure Council page. Sign-up for the newsletter goes to an external list page, which was not opened.

leads_only.name: Fairmount Park Conservancy
leads_only.note: Named as a partner on the Belmont Plateau Trails Alliance site. Its public site lists Belmont Plateau workdays. Not checked as a record in this run because it is a separate organization outside this batch.

leads_only.name: The Discovery Center
leads_only.note: Named on the Black Spatial Relics upcoming events page as the steward of the Strawberry Mansion Reservoir space used for a 2023 lab. No web address on the page.

leads_only.name: The Public Trust
leads_only.note: Named on the Black Spatial Relics pages as the fiscal sponsor of the project. No web address on the page.

notes: All 7 groups in the batch are written as publish records with research_tier 2. Budget: 1 WebSearch (Belmont, the only group whose own site had no further pages) and 26 WebFetch calls of the 42 allowed for this batch. Two pages returned HTTP 404 and were not blocks: belmonttrails.org/about and independencebigs.org/faq. No pages were blocked and no rate limiting was seen. Carried-over corrections: Bicycle Club dues now $20 a year (register page); Ben Franklin newcomer rating 4; Bicycle Coalition newcomer rating 2 (application first); Black Spatial Relics categories and interests changed because the site describes performance work; Big Brothers what_you_do expanded with program details from the programs page. Status moved to active for Ben Franklin, Bicycle Club, Big Brothers and Black Spatial Relics on dated 2026 evidence on each group's own pages. Belmont status is carried over from the city listing and could not be confirmed on the group's own site. Verdict counts: publish 7.
